propensity

pruh-PEN-si-tee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Propensity is a natural tendency to behave in a particular way.

The landlord's insurance rates climbed once the building inspector noted the old wiring's propensity for sparking.

Example

Company records showed the machine had a propensity to overheat during long shifts, a pattern engineers had somehow overlooked for years.

A propensity is a built-in tendency -- something that keeps happening again and again, almost like a habit someone (or something) can't help.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tendency: A tendency is any leaning toward acting or turning out a certain way -- mild or strong, learned or inborn, the loosest word in this family. A propensity is a stronger, more clinical claim: a built-in pattern of behavior, often one on record.

inclination: An inclination is a mild leaning felt by a person -- what you would rather do, a preference that may never turn into action. A propensity is about what actually keeps happening: a natural, repeated pattern of behavior rather than a liking.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aversion: a strong dislike or unwillingness

reluctance: unwillingness or hesitation

Where it sits · how strong the inner pull is — habit → propensity → compulsion

habit vs. propensity: A habit is a specific, learned behavior repeated so often it becomes automatic, while a propensity can be a deeper natural tendency someone was never taught.

compulsion vs. propensity: A compulsion goes even further than a propensity, describing an urge so strong it feels impossible to resist.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forward, toward (Latin)

root — pens-

root — pens-: to hang, to weigh, to incline (Latin pendere)

suffix — -ity

suffix — -ity: state of, quality of (Latin/French)

Put it together

Put it together: Propensity comes from Latin pro- ('forward') + pendere ('to hang, to incline') + -ity -- literally 'the state of inclining toward' something, which is exactly what a natural tendency does.

Use the root in a new word: pendere (the Latin root)

Use the root in a new word: pendere (the Latin root): The same Latin root pendere ('to hang') also hides inside everyday words like suspend and pendant -- both involve something 'hanging.'
